result.summary: This short fragment from the Life of Homer says that Homer, while living with Thestorides, composed the Lesser Iliad and the Phocais. It adds that the Phocaeans claim he composed the Phocais among them.

scenes.title: Homer composes the Phocais
scenes.summary: A biographical note says Homer wrote the Lesser Iliad and the Phocais while living with Thestorides, though the Phocaeans claim the Phocais was written in their city.

characters.name: Homer
characters.description: the poet said to have composed the Lesser Iliad and the Phocais

characters.name: Thestorides
characters.description: man with whom Homer is said to have lived

analysis.text: The fragment shows how ancient biographers attributed many epic poems to Homer and tied them to particular places and patrons. The Phocaeans' competing claim reflects local pride in a connection to the famous poet.
The passage concerns authorship and the uncertain origins of early epic. The Phocais belongs to the group of poems later linked to Homer's name.

fun_facts.text: The Phocais is lost, and it survives only through such short reports about its supposed composition.

language_notes.text: The Lesser Iliad is an epic of the Trojan cycle covering events after Achilles' death; it was traditionally, though doubtfully, attributed to Homer.
Phocaeans are the people of Phocaea, an Ionian Greek city on the coast of Asia Minor.
"The latter" means the Phocais, the second poem named, not the Lesser Iliad.

context_notes.text: Thestorides was a Phocaean schoolteacher-poet in the ancient Lives of Homer, said to have copied Homer's verses and passed them off as his own.
Pseudo-Herodotus is the name given to the anonymous author of a Life of Homer once attributed to Herodotus. Its biographical details are legendary.
